In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
KSHV infection leads to the development of KS by inducing the production of a plethora of viral proteins that have the potential to alter cellular functions.
KS is a multifactorial disease, where the viral genome and its products are essential for the initiation and maintenance of the disease.

KSHV‐encoded genes play a central role in KS pathogenesis, and that they do so in multiple ways, including the induction of cellular genes that are involved in cell proliferation, angiogenesis, inflammation and immune evasion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the viral proteins that we have studied are important for the development of KS lesions.
Kaposi sarcomas are caused by the oncogenic herpesvirus KSHV, and the virus is essential for the development and progression of these tumours.

the viral proteins encoded by KSHV, which are expressed in KS lesions and are responsible for the development of the histological features of this disease, are the result of a complex interaction between the host immune system and the virus, which has evolved over millions of years of co‐evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the KSHV genome encodes a number of viral proteins that are involved in the development of KS lesions.
KSHV‐encoded proteins are responsible for the development of the histological features of Kaposi's sarcoma.
